contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Re-evaluate the strategy whenever query volume, output order, index identity, memory, mutation, hashability, comparability, updates, or worst-case guarantees change.

items.prompt: A static-key membership service changes its query from exact membership to "return every key between a and b in order." How should the preferred structure change?

options.text: The new ordered-range relation favors sorting or another ordered representation.
Exact and range queries are identical for a hash set.
Keep the same strategy because variable names did not change.
Range output never benefits from preprocessing.

feedback.reason: A small change from equality to range semantics crosses the strategy boundary.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Exact membership asks whether one equality class exists, which a set represents directly. A range query asks for lower/upper boundaries and every key between them in ascending order, so it consumes rank and neighboring-key relations.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

A sorted array or ordered index can locate boundaries and traverse a contiguous interval. A plain set has no successor or ascending traversal invariant; a full scan could filter but would need an additional order step. Reusable rule: when the query relation changes, re-evaluate the representation even if the data is identical.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_hash_only: Equality buckets cannot locate the first key at least a, the last key at most b, or traverse successors in order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_names: Variable names are unchanged, but the consumed relation changed from equality to ordered interval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_preprocess: Static ordered preprocessing can be reused to answer many boundary searches and ordered traversals.

items.prompt: A frequency-report task changes from arbitrary group order to ascending key order. What changes in the comparison?

options.text: Sorting becomes directly useful, or the hash path must add key sorting and include that cost.
Output order never affects strategy.
Hash iteration becomes automatically ascending.
Counts must be removed.

feedback.reason: The hash path can remain correct only with an explicit ordering stage.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem
For arbitrary output, a frequency map directly stores k key-count pairs in expected O(n) build time. Ascending output adds an observable relation the table does not guarantee.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

The hash path must sort its k keys, giving expected O(n + k log k), then emit counts in that order. Sorting all n values costs O(n log n) and a run scan emits ordered groups directly. When k ≪ n the hybrid may win; memory or existing order can favor the other path. Reusable rule: add the cost of every newly required output property.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nothing: Two reports with identical counts but different key order are observably different under the new contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_sorted: Bucket or insertion traversal does not universally equal ascending key order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.drop_counts: The contract changed only order; removing multiplicities would make the report incomplete.

items.prompt: A duplicate-detection task adds the requirement to return the earliest repeated arrival index. Which direction does this push?

options.text: Toward a hash-based seen-state scan that preserves arrival order and can stop early.
Toward sorting values without original indices.
Duplicate existence and earliest repeated arrival are the same contract.
Toward checking every pair regardless of constraints.

feedback.reason: Adding an online original-position result changes the consumed structure.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Maintain a set of values from the processed prefix. At index i, test the current value before inserting it; a hit proves i is the earliest repeated arrival because all earlier positions were processed without a repeat.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

For [4,7,4], the set reports index 2 as soon as the final 4 arrives. Offline sorting needs the complete input and decorated indices to reconstruct arrival order; values-only sorting loses it. Duplicate existence alone does not name the earliest second occurrence. Reusable rule: online stopping points require prefix state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.toward_sort_values: Reordered values no longer identify the second original arrival, especially when the same value appears many times.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_change: Existence is a final predicate, while earliest repeated arrival is an order- and position-sensitive event.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_pairs: Pair checks can rediscover equality but ignore the direct prefix invariant and may take O(n²).

items.prompt: A grouping job originally forbids mutation, but the contract changes to allow reordering and imposes a strict auxiliary-memory cap. What transfer is plausible?

options.text: An in-place sort-and-run strategy may become preferable.
The memory cap makes an O(n)-entry hash table automatically better.
Mutation permission never affects memory strategy.
The result must be weakened.

feedback.reason: Allowing mutation changes the sorting path from copy-plus-sort to direct in-place processing.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

When mutation was forbidden, sorting required an O(n) copy to protect the source. Legal reordering removes that copy: a concrete in-place sort can reuse the input array, then one run scan forms groups.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

An in-place heapsort may use O(1) workspace and an introsort O(log n) stack, while a general frequency table can retain O(k)=O(n) entries. The time may rise to O(n log n), but the strict space cap can make this the legal path. Reusable rule: changed mutation permission can change the space model without changing the result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.toward_more_hash: A strict cap weakens a structure that may retain one entry per distinct key.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_effect: Legal in-place writes remove the O(n) protective copy that an immutable sorting path needed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.drop_groups: The same complete grouping result can be produced by sorted runs; weakening output is unnecessary.

items.prompt: A sorted report changes into an online stream that must answer seen-before immediately. Which transfer is appropriate?

options.text: Use incremental hash membership state rather than waiting to sort the complete stream.
Delay every answer until the stream ends.
Binary-search values as they arrive without maintaining order.
Compare only the last two arrivals.

feedback.reason: Online response and arrival order create a lookup-state signal.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem
For each arrival x, a seen set answers immediately whether x occurred in the prefix; then x is inserted for future arrivals. This maintains exactly the relation the new online API consumes.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

Waiting for end-of-stream sorting violates immediate response, binary search lacks maintained order, and comparing only neighboring arrivals misses separated repeats. Reusable rule: when an offline report becomes an online event, switch from final global structure to incremental prefix state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_offline_sort: An answer delivered only after the stream ends fails the requirement to respond on each arrival.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_unsorted: Arrival order provides no half-discard invariant, so binary search cannot decide membership.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacent_only: A stream [a,b,a] repeats a without placing its occurrences next to each other.

items.prompt: Keys stop providing a compatible hash but still provide a total comparator. What should happen?

options.text: Remove the hash strategy from the legal candidate set and use comparison-based ordering where it satisfies the result.
Use an unrelated pointer hash and preserve semantic equality automatically.
The problem becomes unsolvable.
Key operations never affect candidate legality.

feedback.reason: Transfer begins by rechecking which primitive relations exist.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

A correct table requires a hash compatible with semantic equality so an equal lookup reaches the stored entry. Once that primitive disappears, the previous hash strategy is not merely slower—it is no longer a legal implementation.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

The remaining total comparator permits sorting and compare-zero grouping where those structures satisfy the result. Pointer identity and arbitrary strings do not automatically preserve semantic equality. Reusable rule: every transfer starts by revalidating the primitive operations assumed by the old strategy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.invent_hash: Pointer identity can distinguish semantically equal objects, breaking lookup into the same equality class.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_algorithm: The total comparator still supports comparison sorting and ordered equality runs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_cost: Available hash and comparison relations determine which data structures can be correct before costs are compared.

items.prompt: A static sorted dataset becomes highly dynamic with frequent insertions and deletions, while queries remain exact membership only. Which direction can become attractive?

options.text: A hash set can maintain equality state with expected incremental updates, avoiding repeated full resorting.
Full resorting after every update is always optimal.
Frequent updates automatically create ordered range queries.
Updates make reusable state impossible.

feedback.reason: Update frequency changes the lifecycle cost of preprocessing.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

A flat sorted snapshot is reusable only until an update changes its contents. Fully resorting n values after each of u updates can cost O(un log n), while a set can apply hashable insertions and deletions incrementally under expected-operation assumptions.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

Because queries remain exact membership, they consume equality rather than order. This can favor a set, though balanced trees or other dynamic ordered structures may be preferable when deterministic guarantees or future ranges matter. Reusable rule: include maintenance, not only query cost, when a static representation becomes dynamic.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.resort_everything: u full rebuilds can multiply preprocessing to O(un log n), overwhelming the workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_required: Insertions and deletions change update frequency, not the stated exact-membership relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_only: Sets and other dynamic indexes can maintain reusable state across legal updates.

items.prompt: A service changes from expected throughput goals to a deterministic worst-case latency requirement under adversarial keys. What transfer may be justified?

options.text: Toward a deterministic comparison-sorting or ordered strategy, unless hashing supplies an explicit protected worst-case guarantee.
Expected O(1) is automatically a deterministic guarantee.
Input control never affects hashing.
Sorting becomes O(1).

feedback.reason: A change in required guarantee can reverse the preferred legal strategy without changing the nominal input size.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Expected O(1) table operations permit slower collision-heavy cases and resizing spikes. Attacker-controlled keys can target those cases unless the table uses a protected scheme with a relevant proved bound.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

A deterministic comparison sort gives a stated O(n log n) preprocessing bound and binary search O(log n) per exact query; another ordered structure may support dynamic operations. These are not O(1), but they can satisfy predictability. Reusable rule: a changed guarantee level requires a new analysis even when n and query semantics stay fixed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_hash_claim: An expected bound is not a deterministic upper bound for each attacker-selected execution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_adversary: Key control can influence bucket collisions and therefore the latency distribution of conventional hashing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_constant: Sorting remains O(n log n), but its deterministic comparison bound may match the new requirement.

items.prompt: An unsorted dataset is replaced by a guaranteed already-sorted dataset, while the task remains grouped ordered output. What transfer is appropriate?

options.text: Drop both hash construction and sorting; scan existing equal runs directly.
Build a table because hashing is always faster.
Pay O(n log n) to recreate the same order.
Sorted input cannot contain duplicates.

feedback.reason: Input preconditions are reusable work.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

The guaranteed sorted input already places equal keys in contiguous runs and in output order. A single scan counts each run and emits its group, costing O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state excluding output.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

A table rebuild adds expected O(n) work and O(k) entries; sorting again adds O(n log n) work without changing the invariant. Sorted input can still contain adjacent duplicates. Reusable rule: transfer can remove preprocessing entirely when the new input contract supplies the needed structure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_rebuild: The scan already has equality adjacency and key order, so a table adds memory without a needed relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_again: Recomputing an invariant already guaranteed by the input performs unnecessary O(n log n) work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_groups: Sorted order groups equal occurrences next to one another; it does not imply all values are unique.

items.prompt: Which contract changes can reverse a hash-versus-sort decision? Select all that apply.

options.text: Changing arbitrary output to ordered output.
Changing equality lookup to range or successor queries.
Changing mutation permission or auxiliary-memory limits.
Renaming a variable from map to values.

feedback.reason: Strategy transfer follows semantic and resource changes.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Changing arbitrary to ordered output makes rank observable. Changing equality to ranges or successors replaces one-key lookup with ordered-neighbor relations. Changing mutation or memory can make a copy, table, or in-place representation legal or impossible.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

Each accepted change modifies either the structure consumed by the result or the legal resource model, so it can reverse a decision. Renaming a variable changes neither semantics nor cost. Reusable rule: transfer follows a changed invariant or constraint, not changed vocabulary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_rename: The same data, operations, output, guarantees, and resources remain, so no decision boundary moves.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.output_order: Key rank becomes an observable result property, making sorted traversal or an added ordering stage necessary.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.query_relation: Range and successor queries consume boundaries and neighbors that equality buckets do not provide.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.mutation_memory: A copy, O(k) table, or in-place sort can enter or leave the legal candidate set.

items.prompt: After a contract change, which resulting workloads move the decision toward hashing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Immediate seen-before answers in arrival order.
Many arbitrary-order key-count queries on static hashable data.
Frequent exact-membership updates and queries under accepted expected guarantees.
Repeated ordered range reports.

feedback.reason: Hash-favoring transfers introduce equality-heavy, online, or dynamic workloads without ordered output.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Seen-state answers an arrival-prefix equality question immediately. A retained frequency map amortizes one build across many arbitrary-order count queries. A set can also maintain exact membership incrementally through accepted expected insert/delete operations.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

All three accepted workloads consume equality and do not require key order. Ordered range reports instead need boundaries and traversal by rank. Reusable rule: movement toward hashing is justified by equality-heavy reuse, not merely by workload size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_ranges: A plain table cannot locate or traverse a deterministic key interval, while an ordered representation can.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.online_seen: The set summarizes the processed prefix and answers before the remaining stream exists.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.many_counts: One key-to-count table answers each later equality query without rescanning occurrences.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.dynamic_membership: Expected insertions and deletions maintain the exact relation the queries consume without full resorting.

items.prompt: Which contract changes move the decision toward sorting? Select all that apply.

options.text: Counts must now be emitted in key order.
The query changes to nearest values by magnitude.
Mutation becomes legal and a strict memory cap disallows a large table.
The earliest repeated arrival must be returned online.

feedback.reason: Sorting-favoring transfers add ordered relations or make its memory tradeoff legal.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Ordered groups consume ascending runs. Closest-by-magnitude pairs become adjacent candidates after sorting, turning a global search into a local scan. If mutation is legal, an in-place sort can trade O(n log n) time for much less auxiliary state than a general table.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

An online first-repeat event cannot wait for global sorting and instead consumes incremental seen state. Reusable rule: movement toward sorting comes from rank, adjacency, or a newly legal in-place space tradeoff.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_repeat_stream: Reporting before stream end requires prefix membership and an arrival stopping point, which offline sorting cannot preserve directly.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_groups: Sorting establishes both contiguous equality runs and the required key order in one representation.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.closest_pair: In one dimension, any closest pair is adjacent in sorted order, so a linear neighbor scan becomes sufficient.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.tight_memory_mutable: Reusing input storage can avoid the O(n)-entry state that violates the cap.

items.prompt: Which workloads can justify a hybrid representation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Many exact queries plus periodic ordered output.
Frequency updates followed by ordered group emission.
Updates and range queries when both equality and order structures must be maintained.
Exactly one simple membership scan with no reuse.

feedback.reason: Some contracts consume both equality and order strongly enough to justify maintaining both structures.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Many exact queries plus periodic ordered output can use a set/map for equality and a sorted key view for traversal. Frequency updates followed by ordered emission can count in a map then sort only k keys. Dynamic equality and range workloads may maintain both indexes or choose one dynamic ordered structure.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

A hybrid is justified only when both relations are reused enough to repay additional memory, synchronization, and update work. One scan with no reuse needs neither duplicate structure. Reusable rule: combine structures because two relations are independently consumed, not as a default hedge.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_scan_only: With no reuse, building and synchronizing two indexes adds cost without a second operation that consumes them.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.membership_and_order: The equality index serves frequent lookups while the ordered view serves periodic rank-based output.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.counts_then_sorted_keys: Aggregation costs expected O(n), then ordering only k distinct keys costs O(k log k).
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.dynamic_ranges: Equality and range operations may justify synchronized indexes, though one balanced ordered structure is an alternative to compare.

items.prompt: Which tests demonstrate real transfer rather than memorized labels? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the data fixed but change equality lookup into an ordered range query.
Keep the result fixed but change mutation, memory, or guarantee constraints.
Keep semantics fixed but change one query into a large repeated workload.
Rename functions while keeping all semantics and costs fixed.

feedback.reason: Transfer is shown when a controlled change causes a justified strategy update.

blocks.text: Transfer the rule to a new problem

Keeping data fixed while changing equality to ranges isolates the consumed relation. Keeping the result fixed while changing mutation, memory, or guarantees isolates legality. Keeping semantics fixed while increasing q isolates amortization.

blocks.title: Choose the structure the next step needs
blocks.text: Use hash state when the next operation is equality lookup, membership, or arbitrary-order aggregation. Use sorting when the next operation needs ordered keys, adjacent equal runs, intervals, or deterministic traversal. If both are used, include the cost and purpose of each stage.

In each accepted test, one controlled boundary changes and the strategy explanation must follow that change. Renaming functions changes no premise and therefore tests label association rather than transfer. Reusable rule: demonstrate transfer with controlled counterfactuals.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rename_only: All semantics, resources, and lifecycle costs remain identical, so a different choice would be unjustified.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.same_data_new_query: The controlled difference reveals whether the learner selects the structure consumed by the new relation.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.same_query_new_constraints: The same output must now be produced by a different set of legal representations.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.same_contract_new_volume: Increasing reuse changes total build-plus-query costs without changing correctness.

items.prompt: Arrange the general transfer decision process.

elements.text: Identify exactly what changed in result, queries, updates, guarantees, order, indices, memory, or mutation.
Re-evaluate legal key operations and correctness for hashing and sorting.
Recompute complete lifecycle time, peak auxiliary space, and output cost.
Keep or change the strategy with an explicit boundary-based explanation.

feedback.reason: A transfer decision is a delta analysis, not a fresh keyword guess.

blocks.text: Treat transfer as a delta analysis

items: Diff the old and new contracts: result, query relation, update volume, guarantee, order, indices, memory, and mutation.
Recheck correctness and legal primitives; a changed hashability, observability, or online requirement can remove a former candidate.
Recompute complete build, query, update, output, key-operation, and peak-space costs from the new starting representation.
Keep or change the strategy and name the exact boundary whose change explains the decision.

blocks.text: Recomputing costs before checking legality can optimize an invalid path; choosing before either step is a label guess. Reusable rule: changed premise → legal candidates → new formulas → justified transfer.

items.prompt: Arrange the transfer from arbitrary-order counts to ordered groups.

elements.text: Record that the original hash map served arbitrary-order key counts.
Add ascending key order to the output contract.
Choose using k, n, memory, mutation, and guarantee assumptions.

feedback.reason: The added ordering stage changes both mechanisms' complete costs.

blocks.text: Add order, then compare two complete paths

items: Record the old contract: expected-linear hash counting directly served arbitrary-order key-count output.
Add the new observable: groups must now be emitted in ascending key order.
Derive hash-count-plus-sort-k-keys as expected O(n + k log k) and sort-n-values-plus-run-scan as O(n log n).
Choose using k versus n, table and sort workspace, mutation legality, existing order, and required guarantees.

blocks.text: Skipping the new requirement leaves the hash path incomplete; assuming k=n hides the hybrid's advantage when few keys repeat heavily. Reusable rule: transfer formulas should expose the parameter introduced by the changed contract.

items.prompt: Arrange the transfer from offline sorted grouping to online first-repeat detection.

elements.text: Recognize that the complete input is no longer available before answers are required.
Make arrival order and earliest repeated position part of correctness.
Use incremental equality membership with original-position metadata.
Return when the first repeated arrival is observed.

feedback.reason: The online contract invalidates the former sort-first workflow.

blocks.text: Replace final-order state with prefix state

items: Remove the offline assumption: the full stream is unavailable when each answer is due.
Make arrival order and the earliest second occurrence observable parts of correctness.
Maintain incremental seen membership and any required earlier-index metadata over the processed prefix.
On the first membership hit, return the current arrival position immediately.

blocks.text: Sorting first is impossible before the stream ends, while stopping before defining arrival identity cannot identify the requested event. Reusable rule: online transfer changes both the valid state invariant and the time at which correctness must be established.

items.prompt: Arrange a justification for an unfamiliar hash-versus-sort problem.

elements.text: Name the required equality, ordering, grouping, range, or identity relation.
Name output order, indices, mutation, and guarantee requirements.
Model preprocessing, queries, updates, memory, and output size.
Choose or combine strategies and state the condition that would reverse the decision.

feedback.reason: A transferable explanation exposes the mechanism and reversal condition.

blocks.text: Build a mechanism-based justification

items: Name the relation consumed by the task: equality, rank, adjacency, grouping, range, or occurrence identity.
Name every observable constraint: output order, original indices, mutation, online timing, and guarantee level.
Model preprocessing, queries, updates, key operations, peak memory, and output size for each legal representation.
Choose or combine strategies, then state one concrete changed condition that would reverse the decision.

blocks.text: A problem label cannot substitute for these premises. The reversal condition proves the explanation is conditional and transferable rather than memorized. Reusable rule: mechanism + observables + lifecycle + boundary.

items.prompt: One exact-membership query is made on an unsorted array of n values. Compare direct scan, hash-set build plus one query, and sort plus binary search.
constraints: Comparison sorting costs O(n log n).

feedback.reason: For one equality query, a scan and a hash build have the same asymptotic time, but the scan avoids O(n) retained table state.

blocks.text: One query cannot amortize a reusable build

A missing target makes the direct scan inspect n values, so scan time is O(n). Building a set performs n expected O(1) insertions and one expected O(1) lookup, giving O(n + 1)=O(n) expected hash time.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and one binary search adds O(log n), so sort time is O(n log n + log n)=O(n log n). The scan and hash build tie asymptotically, but the scan avoids O(n) retained table state; sorting becomes justified only if another requirement consumes order. Reusable rule: q=1 exposes build cost directly.

items.prompt: A static n-value dataset receives q exact-membership queries. Compare expected hash preprocessing with sort-and-binary-search preprocessing.
constraints: Expected hash build is O(n) and query O(1).
The in-place sort costs O(n log n) and uses O(log n) stack; each binary search costs O(log n).

sort_time: O(n log n + q log n)
O(n log n + q log n)

sort_time.ordered_workload: O(n log n + q log n)

feedback.reason: For equality-only queries under expected assumptions, hashing has the stronger time expression but uses more auxiliary state.

blocks.text: Derive time and space for both retained representations

Hashing builds from n values in expected O(n) time and answers q queries in expected O(q), totaling O(n + q); an all-distinct set retains O(n) entries. The in-place sort costs O(n log n), q binary searches add O(q log n), and its stated stack gives O(log n) auxiliary space.

Thus the sort path is O(n log n + q log n) time and O(log n) space under legal mutation. Hashing has the stronger expected equality-only time expression but spends more state. Existing order, deterministic guarantees, or ordered follow-up queries can reverse the product decision. Reusable rule: compare complete formulas rather than strategy names.

items.prompt: Produce ordered frequency groups from n values with k distinct keys. Compare hash counting plus sorting k keys with sorting all n values and scanning runs.
constraints: Input mutation is legal and required output storage is excluded from auxiliary space.
The in-place comparison sort costs O(n log n) and uses O(log n) stack.

feedback.reason: The transfer decision can depend on k as well as n.

blocks.text: Expose k in the hybrid path

The hash path performs n expected O(1) count updates, stores k entries, sorts only those k keys in O(k log k), and emits them in order. Its time is expected O(n + k log k) and auxiliary space O(k), excluding required output.

The in-place sort orders all n values in O(n log n), the run scan adds O(n), and the stated stack gives O(log n) auxiliary space. Thus sort time is O(n log n). Small k favors the hybrid's time; tight memory, existing order, or guarantee requirements can favor sort-and-run. Reusable rule: distinct-state cardinality can control a hybrid even when input length controls the direct sort.

items.prompt: A dataset undergoes u complete versions, each with n values, and receives q exact queries total. Compare rebuilding a hash set for each version with sorting each version.
constraints: Expected hash rebuild is O(n); hash query is expected O(1).
Each sort is O(n log n); binary-search query is O(log n).

sort_time: O(un log n + q log n)
O(un log n + q log n)

sort_time.resorts_queries: O(un log n + q log n)

feedback.reason: Version churn multiplies preprocessing cost and may reverse a decision based only on static query cost.

blocks.text: Version churn multiplies preprocessing
Each of u versions requires a new expected O(n) set build, totaling expected O(un); q expected O(1) queries add O(q), so hash time is O(un + q).

Sorting each version costs O(n log n), totaling O(un log n), and q binary searches add O(q log n), so sort time is O(un log n + q log n). These formulas assume complete rebuilds; incremental updates, ordered queries, and guarantee requirements would change the model. Reusable rule: multiply preprocessing by every version that invalidates it.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Re-evaluate the strategy whenever query volume, output order, index identity, memory, mutation, hashability, comparability, updates, or worst-case guarantees change.
